name: Battle of Lepanto
info: On 7 October 1571 the Holy League fleet under John of Austria defeated the Ottoman fleet in the Gulf of Patras; the Ottomans rebuilt quickly, and Venice made peace with them in 1573 and gave up Cyprus.

facts.place: The Gulf of Patras, off the Greek coast near Lepanto (ancient Naupactus, Turkish İnebahtı), in present-day Greece
facts.sides: The Holy League, led by Spain and Venice, under John of Austria: 206 galleys and six galleasses, with about 30,000 fighting troops and 40,000 sailors and oarsmen. The Ottoman Empire under Ali Pasha: 211 galleys and 63 galliots, with about 37,000 to 41,000 oarsmen, virtually all of them slaves, and up to 34,000 soldiers.
facts.outcome: The Holy League captured 117 Ottoman galleys and sank or destroyed some 83 others. Losses were about 7,500 dead for the Christians and about 30,000 for the Ottomans, though other sources give 10,000 and 40,000.

t: Lepanto was fought between rowing ships, the last major engagement in the Western world of that kind, and was in essence an infantry battle on floating platforms.
Both fleets depended on oarsmen who were largely enslaved, convicts or prisoners, and some of those freed from Ottoman galleys took up arms during the fighting.
The victory won no territory back: Venice accepted peace in March 1573 and ceded Cyprus, and the Ottomans rebuilt their fleet within months.
dyk: Ali Pasha is supposed to have promised his Christian galley slaves their liberty if he won, while on the Holy League side the galley slaves were freed from their chains before the fighting began.
ev: Nicosia and other Venetian possessions on Cyprus fall to the Ottomans
Famagusta surrenders on 1 August, and the pope's blessed banner reaches Naples on 14 August
The Holy League fleet leaves Messina on 15 and 16 September, then learns that the Ottomans have moved to Lepanto
On 7 October the fleets meet in the Gulf of Patras and the fighting begins around noon
Pope Pius V dies and the League begins to unravel
Occhiali sails with 200 newly built ships and skirmishes with Colonna's fleet
Venice makes peace with the Ottomans on 7 March, ending the War of Cyprus and the Holy League

sections.background:
The Holy League was promoted by Pope Pius V to rescue Famagusta, the Venetian colony on Cyprus, besieged by the Ottomans in early 1571 after the fall of Nicosia and other Venetian possessions in 1570. On 1 August the Venetians surrendered after being assured that they could leave Cyprus freely. The Ottoman commander Lala Kara Mustafa Pasha, who had lost some 50,000 men in the siege, broke his word, imprisoned the Venetians and had Marco Antonio Bragadin flayed alive.

The League's members were the Republic of Venice, the Spanish Empire with its Italian kingdoms, the Papal States, the Republic of Genoa, the Duchies of Savoy, Urbino and Tuscany, the Knights Hospitaller and others. All of them saw the Ottoman navy as a threat to Mediterranean trade and to continental Europe. Spain was the largest financial contributor, though the Spaniards would have preferred to keep most of their galleys for their own wars against the sultanates of the Barbary Coast.

The fleet was placed under John of Austria, half-brother of Philip II of Spain, with Marcantonio Colonna as his principal deputy. The contingents met the Venetian force under Sebastiano Venier at Messina in July and August 1571. On the Ottoman side, Sultan Selim II had issued express orders to destroy the Christian fleet.
sections.forces:
The Holy League had 206 galleys and six galleasses, large new galleys with masts, sails and heavy artillery that the Venetians had developed. Venice supplied 109 galleys and all six galleasses, Spain and its territories 49 galleys, Genoa 27 and the Papal States seven. The fleet carried about 30,000 fighting troops, among them 7,000 Spanish infantry, 7,000 German landsknechts, 6,000 Italian mercenaries in Spanish pay and 5,000 Venetian soldiers, and was manned by 40,000 sailors and oarsmen. The historian George Finlay estimated that over 25,000 Greeks fought on the League's side, as soldiers and as sailors or oarsmen.

The Ottoman fleet under Ali Pasha, with the corsairs Mehmed Sirocco and Uluç Ali, had 211 galleys, 63 galliots and smaller vessels. Its oarsmen, about 37,000 to 41,000, were virtually all slaves, many of them Christians captured earlier. It had 13,000 experienced sailors and 25,000 soldiers, though the number of soldiers may have been up to 34,000, and was short of janissaries. Christians are estimated to have had 1,815 guns and the Ottomans 750, with insufficient ammunition. The Ottomans relied on composite bowmen, the League on arquebusiers and musketeers.

John of Austria mixed the nationalities in each squadron, and sailed from Messina in formation. Divisions of 53, 62 and 53 galleys stood from north to south, with a reserve of 38 under Álvaro de Bazán. The Ottomans stood in three divisions under Sirocco, Ali Pasha and Uluç Ali.
sections.course:
The wind was at first against the League, but around noon it shifted in its favour. Galleasses stationed in front of its line opened fire at close quarters on the foremost Ottoman galleys and confused their order. First contact came around noon between the squadrons of Agostino Barbarigo and Sirocco near the northern shore. Sirocco, who knew the depth of the water, got galleys between Barbarigo and the coast. The ships came so close that they formed an almost continuous platform of hand-to-hand fighting. Barbarigo was killed by an arrow to the eye, but Bazán arrived with the reserve, and Sirocco was killed and beheaded. Christian galley slaves freed from Ottoman ships were given arms and joined in.

In the centre Ali Pasha's galley drove into John of Austria's Real as far as the fourth rowing bench, and Spanish infantry and janissaries fought around the two flagships. Colonna came alongside and helped to push the Ottomans off the Real. The Ottoman flagship was boarded and its entire crew killed, Ali Pasha among them. After two hours the Ottomans were beaten on the left and in the centre, though fighting went on for two more.

On the League's right, Gianandrea Doria sailed south instead of taking his station. He later said he was trying to prevent an enveloping move, but his captains took his signals for treachery. Uluç Ali then fell on the gap and on the flagship of the Knights of Malta, until Bazán's reserve again came up and he retreated with the Knights' flag. Many Greek rowers on Ottoman galleys are said to have mutinied and delivered their ships to the League.
sections.aftermath:
At the end of the battle the Holy League had captured 117 galleys and sunk or destroyed some 83 others. Around ten thousand Ottomans were taken prisoner, and many thousands of Christian slaves were rescued. The League lost around 7,500 dead and the Ottomans about 30,000, while other sources put the figures higher, at 10,000 Christians and 40,000 Ottomans. Celebrations in Rome and Venice included triumphs and pageants with Turkish slaves in chains.

The Ottomans rebuilt fast. About six months later they had built more than 150 galleys, eight galleasses and 250 ships in all, and Occhiali sailed with 200 of them in July 1572. The League did not take advantage of its victory. After the death of Pius V on 1 May 1572 its diverging interests showed, an attack on Navarino was abandoned, and in 1573 the fleet did not sail, John of Austria taking Tunis instead. Venice, fearing for its Dalmatian possessions and eager to resume trade, negotiated alone. The peace of 7 March 1573 disbanded the League and ended the War of Cyprus. Cyprus was ceded to the Ottomans, Venice agreed to pay 300,000 ducats, and the Ottomans occupied fertile parts of the hinterland in Dalmatia.

In 1574 the Ottomans retook Tunis. The Grand Vizier Sokollu Mehmed Pasha is quoted as telling a Venetian envoy that in winning Cyprus the Ottomans had cut off an arm, while in defeating their fleet the League had only shaved a beard.
sections.sources:
The first comprehensive account of the war was Giovanni Pietro Contarini's History of the Events, published in 1572, a few months after the battle, and the only full historical account by an immediate commentator. It praises the victory, but also examines its meaning and the political philosophy of conflict in the early modern Mediterranean. Venetian and Spanish prints, poems and paintings of 1571 and after, among them 233 Italian poems printed between 1571 and 1573, show how the Christian side saw the battle.

The figures vary. The strength of the Ottoman soldiers is given as 25,000 and as perhaps up to 34,000, and the losses as 7,500 and 30,000 or as 10,000 and 40,000. The speeches attributed to the commanders are given with hedges: Ali Pasha is supposed to have promised the galley slaves their liberty, and the janissaries' throwing of oranges and lemons is something that is said. Doria's conduct on the right is also a matter of interpretation, since he gave one explanation and his captains another.

Historians also differ over the weight of the battle. Paul K. Davis calls it more a moral than a military victory. Others have compared it to Salamis. It was often named as the turning point of Ottoman expansion, though this was by no means an immediate consequence, because the League did not recover any lost territory and the Ottomans rebuilt, reasserting supremacy in the eastern Mediterranean.
sections.legacy:
The League credited the victory to the Virgin Mary, whose help it had asked for through the Rosary. Pius V instituted the feast of Our Lady of Victory, which the Catholic Church now celebrates as the feast of Our Lady of the Rosary. Greek Orthodox Christians of Nafpaktos credit the victory to the Panagia Nafpaktiotissa. Philip II used it to strengthen his position as defender of Christendom, and it was of great symbolic importance while Europe was torn by wars of religion.

The battle confirmed the division of the Mediterranean into an eastern half under firm Ottoman control and a western half under the Spanish Crown and its Italian allies, and it halted Ottoman encroachment on Italian territories. Yet the loss of many experienced crews made Ottoman maritime ventures harder after 1580. The galleon would displace the galley, which Lepanto was the last major engagement to depend on, and the Barbary corsairs went on raiding western coasts until the 19th century.

Paintings by Veronese and Titian and in the Doge's Palace, the statue of John of Austria in Messina, motets, and epics by Juan Latino and others commemorate it, as does the poem by James VI of Scotland, written about 1585. G. K. Chesterton's poem of 1911 connects the battle with Cervantes, who also fought in it. In 1942 Elizabeth Goudge used the battle in a war-time novel to call up British resistance to Nazi Germany.

summary: At Lepanto on 7 October 1571 a fleet of the Holy League, led by Spain and Venice, defeated the Ottoman fleet in the Gulf of Patras. Galley slaves served on both sides. The League did not follow up the victory, and by the peace of 1573 Venice ceded Cyprus to the Ottomans.
notes: The article's account of the Ottoman side is thin and comes through Christian sources; the sources section says so and mentions that Ottoman accounts are not offered in the article.

Figures differ inside the article: galleasses are six in the order of battle, but 'four galeasses' are said to open the fight; the central division is 62 galleys and 'another 16 Spanish and Neapolitan galleys' within it. I used 62 and did not mention the four.
Ottoman soldiers: 25,000 (plus a few thousand North African) and 'may have been up to 34,000'; both are given.
Famagusta: the article states flatly that Lala Kara Mustafa broke his word and had Bragadin flayed alive; told as the article tells it. No Ottoman version is given.
The article's list of Holy League ships (Greek galleys from the Ionian Islands, 12) was left out.
The sentence on Ottoman accounts in the sources section is my statement about the source; the editor may want to rephrase.
Not found in the article: the number of Christian slaves freed, a bibliography (the Bibliography section is empty), Ottoman primary sources, the Ottoman view of why the battle was lost.
